steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for a paper presenting LAST-Straw, our annotated 3D spatio-temporal dataset of strawberry plants for automated phenotyping. Explain the breeding and phenotyping background, the need for 3D and temporal data, the dataset gap, and what the paper contributes.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
- Plant breeding and the difficulty of phenotyping strawberry
- Computer vision, 3D perception and phenotyping
- Temporal observation and temporal phenotypes
- Lack of datasets
- Breeders as end users; ground truth and digital phenotypes
- Strawberry phenotyping gap
- Our contribution: LAST-Straw

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
- Breeding
  - breeders screen all progeny at right moment, select on observed phenotypes
  - strawberry: populations up to 20,000 genetically unique individuals
  - many complex phenotypes: flowering time, floral organ structure, truss complexity, peduncle length, fruit display, sweetness, fruit colour/shape/size, canopy architecture, runners
  - repeated observations; short fruiting window -> qualitative selection misses variation (cite)
- Vision and 3D
  - computer vision and sensing -> high-throughput phenotyping tools (cite)
  - 3D perception: more exploration of plant/organ geometry (cite)
  - 3D data substantially improves measurement accuracy of plant structures (cite)
- Temporal
  - automation -> higher observation frequency; associating observations across time captures temporal variation in morphology
  - one study (cite): need for whole-of-lifecycle phenotyping, novel temporal phenotypes (emergence timing of new organs, growth rates)
- Datasets
  - access to relevant datasets is ubiquitous challenge (cite)
  - collection/annotation time-consuming, many man-hours
  - free sharing of 3D point cloud datasets essential (cite)
  - 3D spatio-temporal crop datasets limited to few species (Sec. 2)
- End users
  - breeders select trait combinations for propagators, growers, retailers, consumers
  - tool developers should consider this
  - evaluation against ground truth rare (e.g. cite), effort of ground truth
  - gap traditional vs digital phenotypes: quantitative descriptors (cite), abstract traits (cite)
  - automation -> frequent, comprehensive, quantitative observation of whole populations -> capture genetic variation, more selection precision
- Strawberry
  - speciality berry crop, major economic importance (cite)
  - automated phenotyping relatively unexplored; mostly fruit and phenology; peduncle length not addressed (cite)
- LAST-Straw
  - 3D spatio-temporal dataset, two varieties (6 plants, 14 time steps)
  - semantic + instance annotations for 13 plants; 'in silico' ground truth stem skeletons (267)
  - phenotyping pipeline (Sec. 4), benchmarks vs ground truth: organ counts, plant volume, leaf area, stem length
  - assessing skeletonisation through phenotyping lens
  - Sec. 5: tracking organ instances over time -> tracking phenotypes
  - highlight challenges and future research areas

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Plant breeders want to screen all the progeny in a breeding population at the right moment, so they can observe all the favourable characteristics of each individual and then make a selection decision based on the phenotypes they observed. In strawberry variety development this is a challenge, because breeding populations can have up to 20,000 genetically unique individuals and there are many complex, agronomically important phenotypes, including flowering time, structure of floral organs, complexity of fruit trusses, length of peduncles, display of fruit, sweetness, fruit colour, shape and size, canopy architecture and production of runners, and these are only some of the traits. The observations have to be made repeatedly to evaluate all the essential characteristics, and the window when the plants are fruiting is short, so the traditional qualitative selection by breeders often does not capture all the variation that could be observed in a breeding population.

Developments in computer vision and sensing have led to more and more high-throughput phenotyping tools. More recently, developments in three-dimensional (3D) perception have also shown promise for phenotyping, because they allow more exploration of the geometry of the plant or its organs. This is especially important for doing measurements, and 3D data was shown to improve the accuracy a lot when measuring structures in a plant.

More automation also allows observing more frequently, and being able to associate and integrate observations across time digitally is very important for capturing the large temporal variations in plant morphology. In one study, the authors identify a pressing need for this kind of whole-of-lifecycle phenotyping and they call for developing and studying new temporal phenotypes, which are traits that are dynamic by definition, like the emergence timing of new organs or growth rates.

- Datasets
  - access to relevant datasets is a ubiquitous challenge; collection and annotation cost many man-hours
  - sharing 3D point cloud datasets essential; 3D spatio-temporal crop datasets only for a few species (Sec. 2)
- End users are breeders (propagators, growers, retailers, consumers)
  - evaluation against ground truth rare; traditional vs digital phenotypes (quantitative descriptors, abstract traits)
  - automation could capture genetic variation, increase selection precision
- Strawberry: major economic importance; phenotyping mostly fruit and phenology; peduncle length not addressed
- LAST-Straw
  - two varieties (6 plants, 14 time steps); annotations for 13 plants; 267 ground truth stem skeletons
  - pipeline (Sec. 4) with benchmarks: organ counts, plant volume, leaf area, stem length; skeletonisation assessment
  - Sec. 5: organ tracking over time; challenges and future research

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Plant breeders want to screen all the progeny in a breeding population at the right moment, so they can observe all the favourable characteristics of each individual and then make a selection decision based on the phenotypes they observed. In strawberry variety development this is a challenge, because breeding populations can have up to 20,000 genetically unique individuals and there are many complex, agronomically important phenotypes, including flowering time, structure of floral organs, complexity of fruit trusses, length of peduncles, display of fruit, sweetness, fruit colour, shape and size, canopy architecture and production of runners, and these are only some of the traits. The observations have to be made repeatedly to evaluate all the essential characteristics, and the window when the plants are fruiting is short, so the traditional qualitative selection by breeders often does not capture all the variation that could be observed in a breeding population.

Developments in computer vision and sensing have led to more and more high-throughput phenotyping tools. More recently, developments in three-dimensional (3D) perception have also shown promise for phenotyping, because they allow more exploration of the geometry of the plant or its organs. This is especially important for doing measurements, and 3D data was shown to improve the accuracy a lot when measuring structures in a plant.

More automation also allows observing more frequently, and being able to associate and integrate observations across time digitally is very important for capturing the large temporal variations in plant morphology. In one study, the authors identify a pressing need for this kind of whole-of-lifecycle phenotyping and they call for developing and studying new temporal phenotypes, which are traits that are dynamic by definition, like the emergence timing of new organs or growth rates.

A challenge that is everywhere in research on machine vision methods for agriculture is getting access to relevant datasets. Collecting and annotating these datasets takes a lot of time and resources in man-hours. So freely releasing and sharing 3D point cloud datasets is essential for developing the next generation of phenotyping tools. But 3D spatio-temporal datasets of crops only exist for a few species (see Sec. 2).

We should remember that in the end the users of phenotyping tools are plant breeders, who select particular combinations of traits of interest to meet what propagators, growers, retailers and consumers demand. So the developers of automated phenotyping tools need to consider this when they develop them. More and more research is about developing such tools for phenotyping, but evaluating the resulting phenotypes against a ground truth is rare (e.g.), probably because measuring or annotating ground truth data takes a lot of effort. There is also a gap between traditional and digital phenotypes, and digital ones make it easier to report new or modified phenotypes, which are quantitative descriptors or can quantify more abstract traits. Automated phenotyping could allow more frequent, comprehensive and quantitative observations of whole breeding populations, so there is a big opportunity to capture all the genetic variation in those populations, and this could potentially increase the selection precision of breeding a lot.

Strawberries are a speciality berry crop with major economic importance, but automated phenotyping of strawberry is relatively unexplored. So far it was mostly limited to traits about fruit and phenology, and other economically important traits like measuring peduncle length have not been addressed.

The main contribution of this paper is a 3D spatio-temporal dataset of individual strawberry plants of two varieties (6 plants, 14 time steps), and we think it will be useful for developers and researchers of automated phenotyping tools. We provide it together with manually annotated semantic and instance annotations for 13 plants, and manually tuned 'in silico' ground truth skeletons for the stems for these samples (267 in total). The dataset is called LAST-Straw and it addresses the lack of available 3D spatio-temporal data for strawberry plants, giving high-quality data with rich annotations so that automated phenotyping tools can be developed. We also demonstrate a phenotyping pipeline (Sec. 4) and give benchmarks for the phenotypes that can be extracted at each stage against ground truth values, where this is possible. The traits we demonstrate are organ counts, plant volume, leaf area and stem length. We also demonstrate a methodology for assessing skeletonisation results through a phenotyping lens. Finally, in Sec. 5, we show how tracking instances of organs over time would allow tracking particular phenotypes. Throughout the paper we highlight the challenges of doing phenotyping with real-world data and key areas for future research.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
Plant breeders aim to screen all progeny within a breeding population at the appropriate moment to observe all the favourable characteristics of any given individual and make a selection decision based on those observed phenotypes. The challenge with this process in strawberry variety development is that breeding populations can comprise up to 20,000 genetically unique individuals, and there are a range of complex, agronomically important phenotypes including flowering time, structure of floral organs, complexity of fruit trusses, length of peduncles, display of fruit, sweetness, fruit colour, shape and size, canopy architecture and production of runners, to name but a few traits. Observations must be made repeatedly to fully evaluate all essential characteristics, and the window of opportunity when plants are fruiting is short, meaning that traditional qualitative selection by breeders often does not capture all the potentially observable variation within a breeding population [1].

Developments in computer vision and sensing have led to a growing number of high-throughput phenotyping tools [2,3]. More recently, developments in three-dimensional (3D) perception have shown additional promise for phenotyping, allowing for greater exploration of the geometry of the plant or its organs [4]. This is particularly important for performing measurements, where 3D data has been shown to substantially improve accuracy when measuring structures within a plant [5].

Increasing levels of automation also enable higher observation frequencies, and the ability to digitally associate and integrate observations across time is instrumental in capturing the substantial temporal variations in plant morphology. In [6], the authors identify a pressing need for such whole-of-lifecycle phenotyping and call for the development and study of novel temporal phenotypes, i.e. traits that are dynamic by definition, such as the emergence timing of new organs or growth rates.

A ubiquitous challenge in research on machine vision methods for agriculture is access to relevant datasets [7]. The collection and annotation of such datasets is time-consuming and resource-intensive in terms of man-hours. Thus, freely releasing and sharing 3D point cloud datasets is essential to facilitate the development of next-generation phenotyping tools [2]. However, 3D spatio-temporal datasets of crops are limited to a few species (see Sec. 2).

It should be remembered that the ultimate users of phenotyping tools are plant breeders, who select particular combinations of traits of interest to meet the demands of propagators, growers, retailers and consumers. It is thus important that developers of automated phenotyping tools take this into account. A growing body of research focuses on developing such tools for phenotyping, although evaluation of the resulting phenotypes against a ground truth is rare (e.g. [8]), likely due to the large effort required to measure or annotate ground truth data. A gap also exists between traditional and digital phenotypes, with the latter facilitating the reporting of new or modified phenotypes, which are quantitative descriptors [9] or able to quantify more abstract traits [10]. Since automated phenotyping can enable more frequent, comprehensive, quantitative observations of entire breeding populations, the opportunity to capture all the genetic variation within those populations is great and could significantly increase the selection precision of the breeding process.

Strawberries are a speciality berry crop of major economic importance [11], yet automated phenotyping of strawberry remains relatively unexplored. It has so far been largely limited to traits relating to fruit and phenology, and other economically important traits such as peduncle length measurement have not been addressed [12].

The main contribution of this paper is a 3D spatio-temporal dataset of individual strawberry plants of two varieties (6 plants, 14 time steps), which we envision being of use to developers and researchers of automated phenotyping tools. It is provided along with manually annotated semantic and instance annotations for 13 plants, and manually tuned 'in silico' ground truth skeletons for the stems of these samples (totalling 267). The dataset, named LAST-Straw, addresses the lack of available 3D spatio-temporal data for strawberry plants, supplying high-quality data with rich annotations to allow for the development of automated phenotyping tools. We further demonstrate a phenotyping pipeline (Sec. 4) and provide benchmarks, where possible, against ground truth values for the phenotypes that can be extracted at each stage. The demonstrated traits are organ counts, plant volume, leaf area and stem length. We also demonstrate a methodology for assessing skeletonisation results through a phenotyping lens. Finally, in Sec. 5, we illustrate how tracking organ instances over time would allow particular phenotypes to be tracked. Throughout, we highlight the challenges of performing phenotyping with real-world data and key areas for future research.
